title: Shanghai Red-Braised Chicken with Star Anise and Scallions
blurb: Mahogany-glazed thighs simmered in soy, brown sugar and star anise until the sauce turns to lacquer and clings to every piece.

ingredients.item: 1 1/4 lb boneless skinless chicken thighs, halved
3 tbsp Fusia Asian Inspirations soy sauce
6 scallions, cut into 2-inch lengths, whites and greens separated
2 heads baby bok choy, halved lengthwise

steps.text: Pat the chicken thoroughly dry. Heat 1 tbsp oil in a wide skillet over medium-high until it shimmers and thins out, then lay the thighs in a single layer and sear undisturbed until the undersides are deep golden and release from the pan without tugging.
steps.tip: Crowding steams the meat instead of browning it.

steps.text: Push the chicken to one side and drop the ginger coins, smashed garlic and scallion whites into the bare patch. Stir them in the hot fat until they smell sweet and toasty and the garlic edges turn pale gold.
Pour in the soy sauce, sherry and brown sugar along with 1/2 cup water, then drop in the star anise. Scrape the browned bits off the bottom and bring everything to a hard, rolling bubble.
Lower the heat to medium-low, cover, and simmer until the chicken is fork-tender and the liquid has reduced by about half. Turn the pieces once halfway through so both sides take on color.
steps.tip: A lazy blip-blip bubble, not a boil.

steps.text: Nestle the bok choy halves cut-side down into the braising liquid and re-cover. Cook until the stems are crisp-tender and the leaves have collapsed and gone glossy dark green.
While the bok choy steams, heat the frozen jasmine rice according to the bag and fluff it with a fork.
Uncover, raise the heat to medium-high, and boil the sauce down, spooning it over the chicken, until it is syrupy and coats the back of a spoon in a thin sheet.
steps.tip: It thickens further off the heat, so pull it a touch loose.

steps.text: Kill the heat and swirl in the rice vinegar and sesame oil. Fish out the star anise, pile the chicken and bok choy over the rice, and shower with the raw scallion greens.

swap: No dry sherry on hand — use an equal amount of unsweetened apple juice plus an extra splash of rice vinegar.
leftovers: Refrigerate the chicken sitting in its sauce for up to three days; the glaze sets to a jelly cold and re-melts perfectly over fresh rice.

title: Bengali Shorshe Salmon in Mustard-Turmeric Sauce
blurb: Salmon poached in a sharp, sinus-clearing mustard gravy stained gold with turmeric and punctuated by crackling nigella seeds and slit green chiles.

ingredients.item: 1 tbsp Burman's stone-ground or Dijon mustard
3 tbsp mustard oil or other neutral oil

steps.text: Rub the salmon all over with the turmeric and a generous pinch of salt and set it aside while you build the sauce.
steps.tip: The turmeric seasons the fish and stains it a deep marigold.

steps.text: Whisk both mustards with the sugar and 3/4 cup water until completely smooth and pourable, with no thick paste clinging to the whisk.

Heat the mustard oil in a lidded skillet over medium-high until it just begins to wisp smoke, then cut the heat to medium and add the nigella seeds and slit chiles. They should crackle and sputter the instant they hit the oil.
steps.tip: Smoking the oil first burns off its raw pungency.

steps.text: Pour in the mustard slurry, stand back from the fumes, and simmer until it loses its raw bite and thickens just enough to leave a trail behind the spoon.
Slide the salmon in, spoon sauce over the top, cover, and poach over medium-low until the fish flakes when nudged at the thickest part and the center has just turned matte.
While the fish poaches, heat the basmati pouch and tear the cilantro.

Take the pan off the heat, squeeze in half the lime, and let it stand uncovered so the sauce tightens around the fish. Serve over the rice with cilantro, the softened chiles, and the rest of the lime.

swap: No fresh serranos — stir a teaspoon of Green Dragon Hot Sauce into the sauce right at the end.
leftovers: Keep the fish and sauce together for up to two days and rewarm gently over low heat, since a hard boil turns the mustard bitter.

title: Catalan Romesco Shrimp with Blistered Scallions
blurb: Sweet red shrimp seared hard and dragged through a smoky almond-and-roasted-pepper romesco, with charred scallions for scooping.

ingredients.item: 1 lb Raw Argentinian Red Shrimp, thawed and patted dry
1 bag Fire Roasted Peppers & Onions, thawed and drained

steps.text: Warm 3 tbsp olive oil in a skillet over medium and fry one slice of bread, torn into rough pieces, together with the whole garlic cloves until both are golden brown and crisp at the edges.
steps.tip: Fried bread is what gives romesco its body.

steps.text: Scrape the bread and garlic into a food processor with the almonds, drained fire roasted peppers and onions, smoked paprika, sherry vinegar and crushed red pepper. Blitz to a coarse, spoonable sauce with visible flecks of almond, then season with salt.
Wipe the skillet, set it over high heat, and lay the scallions in a single layer. Leave them alone until they blister and blacken in spots, then turn once and char the other side.
steps.tip: You want real black patches, not gentle browning.

steps.text: While the scallions char, pat the shrimp dry a second time and season them with salt.
steps.tip: Wet shrimp steam and turn rubbery.

steps.text: Pile the scallions onto a platter. Add a slick of oil to the ripping-hot pan and lay the shrimp down in one layer, searing undisturbed until the edges turn opaque pink and the bottoms curl.
Flip and cook just until the shrimp are opaque through the middle and springy to the touch.
steps.tip: Argentinian reds cook fast; pull them early.

steps.text: Toast the remaining bread slice, squeeze lemon over the shrimp, and spoon a thick bed of romesco onto each plate. Drag the shrimp and scallions through it and finish with parsley.

swap: Out of Argentinian reds? Any large raw shrimp works, or sear chicken tenders and slice them over the same sauce.
leftovers: Romesco keeps a week in the fridge under a slick of olive oil and is excellent on fried eggs or roast chicken.

title: Venezuelan Pabellon Bowls with Sweet Plantains
blurb: Cumin-scented beef guiso, brothy black beans and caramelized sweet plantains piled over rice with a snowfall of salty white cheese.

ingredients.item: 2 lb Simply Nature Organic Grass-Fed Ground Beef
4 oz Happy Farms queso fresco or feta, crumbled

steps.text: Heat 2 tbsp olive oil in your largest pot over medium-high. Add the onion, bell pepper and a big pinch of salt and cook, stirring now and then, until the vegetables slump completely and the edges catch brown.
steps.tip: This sofrito is the backbone of the dish, so let it go past merely soft.

steps.text: Push the sofrito to the rim, add the beef in the center, press it into a flat slab, and leave it untouched so it browns hard before you break it into crumbles.
Stir in the garlic, cumin and oregano and cook until the spices coat the meat and smell toasted rather than dusty.
Add the tomatoes and Worcestershire, scrape the bottom clean, and simmer uncovered, stirring every few minutes, until the guiso is thick and glossy with no watery pool at the edges.

While the beef simmers, heat the oven to 425F and tip the black beans with all their liquid into a saucepan. Season with salt and a pinch of cumin and simmer until brothy but slightly thickened, smashing a few beans against the side of the pot.
steps.tip: Those smashed beans give the pot body.

steps.text: Spread the frozen plantains on a sheet pan and roast, turning once, until the edges are dark, sticky and caramelized.
Heat the rice pouches in the last few minutes and fluff them into a serving bowl.
Build each bowl in stripes: rice, then guiso, then brothy beans, then plantains, and crumble the queso fresco over the top.

swap: No frozen sweet plantains — halve two very ripe bananas lengthwise and pan-fry them in butter until deeply caramelized.
leftovers: Store the guiso, beans and plantains separately for up to four days; the beef also makes a terrific filling for arepas or tacos.

title: Isan Pork Larb with Toasted Rice Powder
blurb: Fiery lime-soaked minced pork tossed with fistfuls of mint and nutty toasted rice powder, scooped up with ice-cold cabbage leaves.

ingredients.item: 2 tbsp uncooked jasmine or basmati rice
1 tbsp Thai chili flakes or crushed red pepper

steps.text: Toast the raw rice in a dry skillet over medium, shaking the pan constantly, until every grain is the color of weak tea and the kitchen smells like popcorn.
steps.tip: This powder is the soul of larb, so do not skip it.

steps.text: Grind the toasted rice to a coarse sand in a mortar, spice grinder, or a zip-top bag under a rolling pin, then set it aside.
Add 1/4 cup water to the same skillet over medium-high, drop in the pork, and mash it into fine crumbles with the back of a spoon. Cook until no pink remains but the meat still looks moist and loose.
steps.tip: The splash of water keeps the pork tender instead of crusty.

steps.text: While the pork cooks, slice the shallot and scallions, pick the mint leaves, and separate the cabbage leaves into a bowl of ice water so they go glassy and crisp.
Kill the heat and pour in the fish sauce, lime juice, sugar and chili flakes. Stir and taste: it should be aggressively sour, salty and hot, all at once.
steps.tip: Season while the pork is warm so it drinks the dressing in.

steps.text: Fold in the shallot, scallions, most of the herbs and all but a spoonful of the rice powder. The mixture should look glossy and clumped, never soupy.
Pile the larb into a bowl, dust with the reserved rice powder and remaining herbs, and serve with the drained cabbage leaves and hot jasmine rice.

swap: Ground chicken or turkey stands in for pork; add an extra splash of fish sauce to make up for the leaner meat.
leftovers: Larb keeps two days cold and is arguably better straight from the fridge, stuffed into lettuce cups or protein wraps.

title: Danish Frikadeller with Dill Potatoes and Agurkesalat
blurb: Butter-fried pork-and-beef patties perfumed with allspice, served with dill-slicked potatoes and sweet-sour paper-thin cucumbers.

ingredients.item: 1/2 lb Simply Nature Organic Grass-Fed Ground Beef
1 small onion, grated on a box grater

steps.text: Put the potatoes in a pot of cold salted water, bring to a boil over high heat, then cook at a steady simmer until a knife slides into the largest one with no resistance.
While the potatoes cook, toss the cucumber slices with the vinegar, sugar and 1/2 tsp salt and refrigerate. They will go limp and translucent and release a pool of sharp brine.

Grate the onion straight into a bowl, juice and all, then add the pork, beef, egg, flour, allspice, 1 1/2 tsp salt and plenty of pepper. Beat hard with a wooden spoon until the mass turns pale, sticky and springy.
steps.tip: The beating is what gives frikadeller their bounce.

steps.text: Melt 3 tbsp of the butter in a large skillet over medium until it foams. Scoop the meat with a spoon, shape ovals with a wet hand, and set them straight into the foaming butter.
steps.tip: Wet hands keep the mixture from gluing itself to you.

steps.text: Fry undisturbed until the undersides are deep mahogany and a spatula lifts them cleanly.
steps.tip: Keep it at medium; butter scorches above that.

steps.text: Flip and fry the second side until browned and firm when pressed, with no pink at the center of the thickest one.
Drain the potatoes, return them to the hot dry pot, add the remaining butter and most of the dill, and swirl the pot until every potato glistens and a few skins split.
Plate the frikadeller with the dill potatoes and a drained mound of the cucumber salad, then spoon the browned butter from the skillet over the top.

swap: All pork or all beef works fine; with a leaner blend, beat a splash of milk into the mixture to keep the patties juicy.
leftovers: Cold frikadeller are a Danish lunchbox staple — slice them onto rye bread with mustard and the leftover pickled cucumber.

title: Guatemalan Pollo en Jocon
blurb: Chicken simmered in a vivid green tomatillo and cilantro sauce thickened the old way, with toasted pumpkin and sesame seeds.

ingredients.item: 1 (16 oz) jar Casa Mamita salsa verde
1 bunch cilantro, leaves and tender stems

steps.text: Toast the pepitas and sesame seeds together in a dry skillet over medium, shaking often, until the pepitas puff and pop and the sesame turns gold.
steps.tip: Pull them the moment they smell nutty; they scorch in seconds.

steps.text: Blend the toasted seeds with the salsa verde, cilantro, scallions, bell pepper, garlic and coriander until completely smooth and shockingly bright green.
Season the chicken thighs generously with salt. Heat 1 tbsp oil in a wide pot over medium-high and sear them in a single layer until the undersides are well browned.
steps.tip: You are after color here, not doneness.

steps.text: Pour the green sauce over the chicken — it will hiss and spatter — then add the broth and scrape the bottom of the pot clean.
Simmer uncovered over medium-low, stirring occasionally, until the sauce shifts from grass green to a deeper olive and thickens enough to coat the chicken.
steps.tip: That color change is your cue that the raw edge has cooked out.

steps.text: While it simmers, warm the tortillas one at a time in a dry skillet until they puff, soften and speckle, then stack them inside a folded towel.
Shred the chicken into big rough pieces with two forks right in the pot, stir it back through the sauce, and season with salt to taste.
Heat the rice pouch, then ladle the jocon over it with the warm tortillas alongside for scooping.

swap: No salsa verde on the shelf? Simmer a pound of quartered tomatillos with a jalapeno until soft and blend that in instead.
leftovers: The sauce tightens overnight, so loosen it with a splash of broth; it makes an excellent filling for tacos or enchiladas.

title: Big-Batch Andalusian Sherry-Garlic Chicken with Saffron Potatoes
blurb: Two whole heads of garlic melt into a golden sherry and saffron braise with green olives, cumin and lemon — Seville tavern food, scaled up.

ingredients.item: 4 lb bone-in skin-on Kirkwood chicken thighs
2 heads garlic, cloves peeled and smashed

steps.text: Heat the oven to 400F. Pat the chicken bone-dry and salt it heavily on both sides, then let it sit uncovered while the oven comes up to temperature.
steps.tip: Dry skin is the only route to crisp skin.

steps.text: Crumble the saffron threads into 1/2 cup warm water and leave them to bloom into a deep orange infusion.
Heat 2 tbsp olive oil in a large Dutch oven over medium-high and sear the chicken skin-side down in two batches until the skin is bronzed and lifts away without sticking.
steps.tip: Two unhurried batches beat one crowded, steamy one.

steps.text: Move the chicken to a plate. Pour off all but a slick of the fat, add the onion and smashed garlic, and cook over medium until the garlic is soft and golden through, stirring so nothing catches.
steps.tip: Burnt garlic will sour the whole pot.

steps.text: Stir in the cumin and bay leaves for a minute, then pour in the sherry and scrape up every browned bit. Boil hard until the sharp alcohol smell has burned off and the liquid looks syrupy.
Add the potatoes and the saffron water, season with salt, and nestle the chicken back in skin-side up so the skin sits above the liquid.
Slide the uncovered pot into the oven and roast until the potatoes are tender all the way through, the sauce has reduced around them, and the chicken pulls easily from the bone.
steps.tip: Baste the potatoes if you like, but never the skin.

steps.text: Scatter the olives over the top and return the pot to the oven just long enough to heat them through and soften them slightly.
Off the heat, stir the sherry vinegar and lemon juice into the pan sauce, taste for salt, and finish with the lemon zest and parsley.

swap: No sherry — use dry white wine plus an extra tablespoon of sherry vinegar stirred in at the end.
leftovers: Pull the meat off the bones and keep it in the sauce for up to four days; it reheats into a fantastic bocadillo filling.
